idiom_name: url.URL + http.Header/Client with a small Link envelope struct
implementation_notes: The classic hand-rolled structure collapses into two stdlib packages: the link target is a first-class *url.URL (url.Parse per RFC 3986) whose ResolveReference method resolves a relative href against the request URL exactly as RFC 3986 Section 5.2 requires, and the consumer dereferences it with a shared http.Client (or forwards it untouched through httputil.ReverseProxy). What replaces the classic structure is that tiny envelope over stdlib primitives — a hand-written struct Link{Href string `json:"href"`; Rel, Method string} marshaled into the carrier payload, because the stdlib ships no RFC 8288 Link-envelope type and no HATEOAS link generator like ASP.NET Core's LinkGenerator. Emitting the header form is one call (http.Header.Set("Link", ...)); the full link-value wire grammar (quoted-string params, comma-in-target) still justifies a dedicated RFC 8288 Appendix B parser when you must interop on that format. Links survive serialization as plain href strings in JSON; hand the receiver a url.URL value (or MarshalBinary bytes) rather than a shared *url.URL pointer when the transfer is meant to move ownership.
pitfalls: http.Header canonicalizes keys to MIME form (the server canonicalizes incoming header names), so a raw map read h["Link"] misses what Header.Values("Link") finds — always access carrier headers through Get/Values.

http.Client follows up to 10 redirects by default, so dereferencing one link can transparently chase a whole chain; set CheckRedirect and return http.ErrUseLastResponse when the consumer must see each hop or enforce a hop budget.

url.Parse is deliberately lenient (the package docs warn parsing ambiguity may not yield an error), so a malformed href can pass production and fail only at request time; and URL.String re-escapes via EscapedPath — building URLs by string concatenation and then parsing them double-escapes the path.

Marshaling *url.URL with encoding/json serializes the struct fields (Scheme/Host/Path...), not the href — marshal u.String() instead; conversely a bare href string loses rel/method metadata, so keep the rel-keyed Link envelope in the payload.

Dereferencing a received link is not authorization: the default client happily requests whatever absolute href arrived, so validate the resolved URL's scheme and host (u.Scheme, u.Hostname()) against an allowlist before client.Do, or a rel="next" link turns the service into an SSRF pivot against internal topology.
One shared http.Client (docs: create once and re-use) is safe for concurrent goroutines; allocating a client per dereferenced link exhausts sockets and descriptors under load.
